# How Motionade works

Motionade is a layered motion medium in the spirit of After Effects: a film of Scenes, each a stage of objects whose properties change over time through Actions, with masks, Effects and a camera on top. What an agent authors is the same project a person edits in Studio, Motionade's editor, so the structure you choose decides what a person can adjust afterwards. This page says how the parts behave so you can combine them freely; it holds no recipes. To find what serves a particular need, read the `needs` section. For a kind's exact input, conditions and examples that stage, call `listCapabilities` with `kinds` (for example {"kinds": ["addMorph"]}); `operations` lists every kind with its fields.

## The film

A project is the film. Its `format` sets width, height and frame rate (`setProjectFormat`); Scenes, Actions and keys are timed in frames at that rate. The project also holds what its Scenes share: media assets, fonts, timing styles and audio clips.

The film plays its Scenes in order. A Scene is one shot with its own duration, background, objects, Actions, camera, masks and post effects, and its own clock that starts at frame 0. Object and Action ids belong to their Scene, so nothing crosses a cut by itself.

Scenes cut by default. A transition joins two of them (`setTransition`, kinds in `transitionKinds`). With `hold`, the outgoing Scene freezes on its last frame while the incoming one plays, and the film keeps its length; with `overlap`, both play through the transition and the film gets shorter. A `sharedElement` transition carries one object that has the same id in both Scenes.

In Studio, the Scene strip shows the Scenes in order, with a button between each pair for its transition; the timeline shows one Scene.

## Objects

An object is one layer. Its kind is `text`, `shape`, `path`, `image`, `video` or `frame` (`objectKinds`). Each object has three parts:

- `base`, where and how it sits by design: `x` and `y` (its top-left corner in its parent's space), `width`, `height`, `opacity`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotation`, the 3D channels `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `translateZ` and `perspective`, skew, and the origin that scale and rotation turn about (`originX` and `originY`, the centre when absent);
- `style`, how it paints: its fill (`primaryFill`: a solid, a gradient or a Shader), stroke, corner radius, blur, Effects, motion blur, and type settings for text;
- `content`, what it is: the text, the shape's geometry, the path's network, or the media asset.

A top-level object's position is in Scene pixels from the top-left of the film's format, x to the right and y down, and depth (`translateZ`) comes toward the viewer (the axes are in `authoringGuide`, a key of the answer `listCapabilities` gives with no arguments); a child's position is measured inside its Frame (below). Siblings paint in `layer` order, higher in front. A property is one animatable channel of an object, such as `x`, `opacity` or `fill`; section `objectProperties` lists every one with the kinds it applies to. An object's design state is what each property shows when nothing animates it.

In Studio, the Layers panel shows the tree, the canvas moves, resizes and rotates objects, and the Design panel edits the base and the style.

## Frames carry their children

A Frame is the only object that holds others. A child names its Frame with `parentId`, and its `x` and `y` are measured from the Frame's top-left. Moving, scaling, rotating or turning the Frame in 3D carries every child. The Frame's `opacity` fades it and its children as one image; `backgroundOpacity` fades only its own fill and stroke. With `clipChildren` it crops its children to its rounded box. A layer blur or an Effect on a Frame filters the Frame and everything in it as one image. A Frame with no fill and no stroke paints nothing: it only carries. With auto layout (`setAutoLayout`) a Frame places its children in a row or a column.

A child shows only while its Frame exists (see the next sections).

In Studio, the Layers panel nests and reorders layers; the Frame inspector holds the fill, Clip contents and auto layout.

## Actions change properties over time

Motion is made of Actions. An Action changes one or a few properties of one target over a range of the Scene's frames. It carries its catalog id (the catalog is section `actions`), its target, its `timing` (a start frame and a duration), its `stage`, and its facets: one keyframe track for each property it drives. Keys sit at frames counted from the Action's start; between two keys, the earlier key's `outgoingTiming` shapes the change: a named easing, a cubic bezier, a spring, a hold, or a shared timing style. `materializeActionFacets` creates an Action with its whole key list.

The target is an object, the word or letter segments of a Text, a Repeater's copies or its whole field, or the Scene camera. Actions belong to the Scene, not to the object, and their order in the Scene's list matters where two overlap (see below).

Three other kinds of motion block sit beside Actions:

- event Actions happen at one frame: `hide`, `show` and `changeText` (`addEventAction`);
- Effect blocks key the Properties of an Effect or a Shader; Studio makes one when a person keys a Property, `addShader` adds the ramp that drives a Shader's `phase`, and an agent keys the other Properties into the same block with `keyShaderProperty`;
- expression blocks compute values from formulas, time ramps, springs and controls (`addMotionBlock`); a person adjusts one through its controls.

Typed operations build blocks through the product's own planners and leave ordinary editable blocks behind: `addFollowPath`, `addDrawErase`, `addMorph`, `addCameraShot`, `applyPreset` and `applyRecipe`.

Every block has an editability that decides what Studio lets a person change: a `full` or `parametric` block can be restructured; a `transform-only` one can be re-keyed, retimed and deleted; a `locked` one can only be inspected.

In Studio, each object has a lane on the timeline with a row per Action. A person drags an Action to move it, drags its edges to stretch it, drags and edits its keys, and edits each segment's curve in the timing popup.

## Before, during and after an Action

An object exists for one span of its Scene, its lifetime:

- it starts where its earliest Action with stage `in` starts; with no such Action, at the start of its `range` (`setObjectRange`); with neither, at frame 0;
- it ends where its latest Action with stage `out` ends; with none, at the end of its `range`; with neither, at the Scene's end;
- a child's lifetime is cut to its Frame's.

Outside its lifetime an object is hidden and its Actions do nothing.

Inside the lifetime, each property shows its design value as changed by the Actions that write it:

- before an Action starts, it writes nothing; Draw and Erase are the exception and hold their first key, so a line that draws from nothing stays hidden until its Draw starts;
- while it runs, its keys play;
- after it ends, its After decides: `hold` keeps its last value, `release` returns the property to its design value. It is one value per Action, which an agent writes as `persistence` on every facet; `setMotionWritePersistence` changes it later on an Action that writes properties. Draw, Erase, Follow Path and Morph always hold.

So an entrance is an Action with stage `in` whose first keys are where the object comes from (transparent, offset, small) and whose last keys are its design state, held. An exit is an Action with stage `out`: the object is gone when it ends. Events last: after `hide` an object stays hidden until a `show`, and after `changeText` the new text stays until the next change.

In Studio, the timeline shows each object's lifetime as a bar a person can drag, and the Action inspector holds its After.

## How Actions on one property combine

Each facet composes onto its property in one of three ways, fixed by the catalog (each facet's `compose` in section `actions`):

- add: Move, Rotation, Depth Z, Resize and the tilts of 3D Rotate add to the design value (a key's value less its track's `baseValue`), so a drift and a bounce on one object add up;
- multiply: Scale multiplies the design scale, so two Scales multiply;
- replace: Opacity, Background Opacity, Color, Stroke, Shadow, the blurs, Corner Radius, Letter Spacing, Line Height, Font Weight, Content Offset, Layout Spacing and the camera's Actions replace the value.

At one frame a property is the winning replace (or the design value when no replace writes), multiplied by the factors and with the offsets added; an expression block can also clamp the result to a minimum or a maximum. When one channel mixes factors and offsets in expression blocks, a factor listed before the channel's first offset scales the replace and one listed after it scales the sum. Where several replacing Actions write at once, the one later in the Scene's list of Actions wins. The list decides, not time: an Action that has ended and holds still writes, so it beats an earlier-listed Action that runs after it. `reorderMotionBlock` changes the order.

Draw and Erase on one Path combine by time instead: a running one beats a held one, and two running together on the same trails show only what both keep, which is how a Draw plus a reverse Erase makes a travelling stroke. A Follow Path owns the follower's position (and its rotation when oriented) from its start and, because it holds, on until the follower's lifetime ends: no other Action may write those channels in that time, its guide must live as long, and the object takes no second Follow Path in that lifetime.

A child's properties combine on their own; its Frame's transform and opacity then apply on top.

In Studio, dragging an Action's row within an object's lane changes the order.

## Text

A Text's content is its words, its style runs (ranges with their own style) and its segments. Segment mode `word` or `letter` splits it into pieces one Action can schedule: an Action on the segment group with a `segmentSchedule` gives each word or letter its own window (stagger, direction, humanize, per-segment overrides) and derives its own duration from them. Segments animate position, opacity, scale, rotation, blur and fill. A caret (`addTextCaret`) follows a letter schedule's typing. A Text must use a family the server lists in `fonts`; section `fontFaces` lists each family's weights.

In Studio, a person types on the canvas, and edits the schedule in the inspector and each segment's window on the timeline.

## Shapes and paths

A shape is a rectangle, an ellipse, a polygon or a star, or custom geometry that Studio's vector editing makes from one. A path is a vector network: vertices and the segments between them, named stroke trails (the routes a stroke follows, which Draw, Erase, Follow Path and brushes address by id), fill loops, and the regions its lines enclose, which can be painted, merged, subtracted or lifted out as a new path (section `path`). A connector is a path anchored to two objects. A network path's stroke takes a treatment (plain, a dynamic wobble, or a brush) and a width profile. A Morph turns the outline of a shape or a network path into another outline over time (section `geometryMorph`).

In Studio, the pen and pencil draw paths (section `canvasCreation`), and vector edit mode moves points, paints regions, merges and subtracts.

## Many copies

A Repeater turns one object into a field: the object stays the Original, and the engine generates Copies in a line or a grid with variation ramped across them (scale, opacity, rotation, offset, hue). Motion addresses the Original as an ordinary object, all the Copies at once (with a stagger set on each Copies Action), or the whole Field. Copies are generated, never authored, and all show the Original's content (section `repeater`).

## Masks, Effects, blur and the camera sit on top

A mask is a relationship between two siblings in a Scene: a source supplies coverage to a target (`addMaskBinding`). In `vector` mode the coverage is the source's outline (a shape, a path or a Text's glyphs); in `alpha` mode it is the source's painted alpha, which an image or a video can also supply; `inverted` flips it. The source paints nothing itself, and the coverage cuts the target's finished picture, its blur and Effects included. Both stay ordinary objects: animate them, not the binding. Each object belongs to at most one mask, a Frame cannot be a target, and a mask is refused under a projective camera or a 3D pose.

Effects filter an object's painted pixels after its layer blur and motion blur: an ordered stack of native Effects (`glow`, `dropShadow`, `colorGrade`, `outline`, `grain`, added with `addObjectEffect`) and Shader Effects. A Shader (`addShader`) can also be an object's fill (`objectFill`), the Scene background (`sceneBackground`), an Effect on an object (`objectEffect`), a filter on what shows behind an object inside its outline (`objectBackdrop`), or a post effect over the whole composited Scene (`scenePostEffect`). For a Shader of your own: Write the SkSL yourself and decide which of its values a person can retune and keyframe in Studio: each of those is a Property, declared with its control and read in the source as its uniform. Every other value is a constant in the source, which Studio cannot change: it has no SkSL editor. Time is a Property too: there is no time uniform, so declare a number Property and name it in `shader.phase`, and the server drives it with a linear ramp whose speed and offset a person can retune. Check each version with `compileShader` before `addShader`; retune a placed Shader's values with `updateShaderValues`, and key them over time with `keyShaderProperty`.

Blur comes in three kinds: layer blur softens the object itself, background blur softens what shows through a shape or a path, and motion blur (`style.motionBlur`) smears an object's own transform motion over a shutter.

The camera looks at the whole Scene. Its resting pose is set with `setSceneCamera`; camera Actions (`cameraFrame`, `cameraRoll`, `cameraDolly`, `cameraTilt`, `cameraLens`, `cameraFocus`) move it, and `addCameraShot` solves a framing into a Camera Frame Action. The camera is flat (pan, roll and zoom) until a dolly, a tilt or a lens makes it projective; then layers at different depths (`translateZ`) show parallax, and camera focus can blur by depth. Where camera Actions overlap, the later in the Scene's list wins, and a held shot keeps the camera until another takes over (section `camera`).

In Studio: Use as Mask, and the mask's mode and Invert in the inspector; the Effects section and the Motion Blur card; the Scene camera section, and the Camera lane on the timeline where shots are rows with keys.

## Time and order

- Actions, events and lifetimes are placed in Scene frames; keys in frames from their Action's start.
- A spring segment runs in seconds from its left key, so the segment's length does not set its speed.
- An Action can start where another ends, plus a delay (`updateMotionBlockSequencing`), and follows it when that one moves.
- A stagger group offsets several Actions by rank times a delay (`addStaggerGroup`); a motion block group names and retimes one object's Actions together without changing what they do (`addMotionBlockGroup`).
- A timing style is a shared curve that segments reference live (`createTimingStyle`): change the style and every segment that uses it changes.
- Audio clips sit on the film's timeline, not on a Scene's clock; a clip locked to a Scene moves with it.

## After Effects words

| After Effects | In Motionade |
| --- | --- |
| Composition | A Scene; the project is the film, its Scenes in order. |
| Precomp | A Frame: its children transform, fade, clip and take Effects as one. They keep the Scene's clock: there is no nested timeline, and nothing is reused across Scenes. To move one object's Actions in time together, a motion block group (`retimeMotionBlockGroup`). |
| Null object | A Frame with no fill and no stroke, used as a parent. |
| Parenting | `parentId`; only a Frame can be a parent. |
| Anchor point | `originX` and `originY`, as fractions of the box. |
| Track matte | A mask, which names its source instead of taking the layer above: `alpha` mode works as an alpha matte, `vector` mode uses a shape's, a path's or a Text's outline, `inverted` is the inverted matte, and the source is hidden like a matte layer. No luma matte. |
| Layer mask | A mask with a shape or path source, or a Frame's `clipChildren` for a rounded-box window. |
| Adjustment layer | None as a layer. Nearest: an Effect on a Frame filters everything inside it; a Shader on `objectBackdrop` filters what shows behind an object; a `scenePostEffect` Shader filters the whole Scene. |
| Graph editor | Each segment's curve: a named easing, a cubic bezier, a spring or a hold. Studio edits one segment's curve at a time in its timing popup. |
| Hold keyframe | A `hold` segment, Hold in Studio's timing popup. |
| Easy Ease | A named easing such as `easeInOutCubic`. |
| Expression | An expression block (`addMotionBlock`): values from time ramps, springs, controls and arithmetic, sin and cos included. No JavaScript, wiggle, random or loopOut. |
| Essential Graphics | A block's controls (`updateMotionBlockControls`); a shared curve as a timing style. |
| Motion path, auto-orient | Move travels in straight lines between keys; a curved path, oriented or not, is Follow Path (`orientToPath`). |
| Motion blur | Motion blur on the object (`style.motionBlur`), its shutter keyed by the Motion Blur Action; quality for the project with `setMotionBlurQuality`. |
| Trim paths | Draw and Erase Actions on a network path's stroke trails (`addDrawErase`). |
| Merge paths | Merge and Subtract of regions inside one network path (`mergePathRegions`, `subtractPathRegions`); not across separate objects. |
| Shape layer | Shape objects and network paths. |
| Repeater | `addRepeater`, in a line or a grid. |
| Text animator, range selector | One Action on a Text's word or letter segments with a `segmentSchedule`. |
| Sequence layers, stagger | A stagger group (`addStaggerGroup`); sequencing after another Action; a Copies stagger on a Repeater. |
| Effects, layer styles | Native Effects (`glow`, `dropShadow`, `colorGrade`, `outline`, `grain`) and Shader Effects; a shadow keyed over time is the Shadow Action. |
| Solid | A rectangle shape, or the Scene background. |
| Camera layer | The Scene camera and its Actions; `addCameraShot`. |
| 3D layer | `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `translateZ` and `perspective` on any object; the 3D Rotate and Depth Z Actions. |
| Depth of field | Camera focus (`cameraFocus`) on a projective camera with `maxBlurPx` above 0. |
| Layer in and out points | The object's lifetime: In and Out Actions, or its `range`. |
| Mesh warp, puppet | An object's `warp`: a grid whose points are placed by expressions of their grid position (`vertexU`, `vertexV`) and the Scene's time; a Repeater's `fieldWarp` bends the whole field. Studio has no editor for an object's warp. |
| Time remap, loopOut, wiggle | None. Nearest: retime the Actions; sin of a time ramp in an expression block; the `camera-shake` recipe. |
| Blend modes | None. Build light with a Shader or with opacity. |
| Text on a path | None. Nearest: one Text per letter, each on a Follow Path. |
| Render queue | Studio's Export, or the page a `createExportLink` link opens, renders the film on the user's machine; the server renders single frames for checking. |
